CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 110 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 17




         BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

             IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF
             OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC
             COMPANY FOR AN ORDER OF THE
             COMMISSION APPROVING ITS NEW                               PUD2026-000046
             EXTRA LARGE LOAD TARIFF AND TERMS
             AND CONDITIONS OF SERVICE FOR
             EXTRA LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS AND A
             REGULATORY ASSET TO RECOVER
             COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH PORTFOLIO
             OPTIMIZATION SOFTWARE


                                 ATTORNEY GENERAL’S BRIEF-IN-CHIEF

                 Gentner F. Drummond, the Attorney General of Oklahoma (“Attorney General”), on behalf

         of the utility customers of this State, hereby submits this Brief-in-Chief (“Brief”) in the proceeding

         referenced above. Although the Attorney General does not consider his position in this matter to

         be an “Alternative Electric Framework” as described in Order No. 761449, he files this Brief out

         of an abundance of caution to comply with the Procedural Schedule set forth therein.

                 The Attorney General respectfully urges the Oklahoma Corporation Commission

         (“Commission”) to adopt the Accelerated Capacity Support (“ACS”) framework described in the

         responsive testimony of Attorney General witness Frank J. Beling, under which a qualifying large

         load customer may bring a generating resource that Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company

         (“OG&E” or the “Company”) acquires and operates as a system resource, subject to independent

         evaluation and Commission oversight. 1 The ACS framework keeps new generation within

         Oklahoma’s current regulated electric system and offers a lawful, ratepayer-protective path to

         serve large loads.




         1
           Responsive Testimony of Frank J. Beling on Behalf of Gentner F. Drummond, Oklahoma Attorney General
         [hereinafter “Beling Responsive”] 22:10–23:20.

         PUD2026-000046
         Attorney General’s Brief-in-Chief                                                             Page 2 of 17

                                                      I. Background

                 On June 17, 2026, OG&E filed its Application for approval of a new Extra Large Load

         Tariff (“XLPL Tariff”) and terms and conditions of service for Extra Large Load customers, as

         well as a regulatory asset to recover costs associated with portfolio optimization software.

         Responsive, rebuttal, and surrebuttal testimony filed in this proceeding presented various customer

         self-supply proposals and alternative electric service frameworks (collectively referred to herein

         as “AES frameworks”) that OG&E contended present substantial legal and jurisdictional

         questions. 2 The Commission issued Order No. 761449 on October 21, 2026 (the “Order”), granting

         OG&E’s Motion to Amend the Procedural Schedule and establishing a briefing schedule with

         enumerated briefing issues to assist with addressing legal questions in this Case. 3

                 The Attorney General, on behalf of the utility customers of this State, supports the ACS

         framework Mr. Beling described. Mr. Beling illustrated the ACS framework “includes defined

         eligibility requirements, an accelerated independent evaluation, standards for system treatment,

         and appropriate protections if the associated large load does not materialize or departs the

         system.” 4

                 This Brief addresses the Order’s enumerated questions (a)–(n) as they pertain to the

         Attorney General’s position. The Attorney General takes no position on, and does not speak to the

         lawfulness of, the AES frameworks advanced by other parties, except to the extent that a

         comparison illustrates why the ACS framework is lawful and protective of ratepayers.

         Attorney General’s Brief-in-Chief                                                      Page 3 of 17

                                           II. Argument and Authorities

                    The Attorney General’s position is that the ACS framework is lawful, within the

         Commission’s authority, and protective of ratepayers. In support of that position, this Brief

         explores three specific points. First, the Commission possesses ample constitutional and statutory

         authority to approve a framework under which the Company acquires a customer-brought resource

         as a system resource. Second, the ACS framework is consistent with House Bill 2992 and the cost

         causation mandates of Title 17 of the Oklahoma statutes, both of which govern this proceeding.

         Third, because the ACS framework keeps generation within the regulated, vertically integrated

         system and leaves the Company as the exclusive retail supplier, it does not implicate the Retail

         Electric Supplier Certified Territory Act, Oklahoma’s retail-competition statutes, or retail

         wheeling.

         A.        The Commission has broad constitutional and statutory authority to approve the ACS
                   framework, and the framework is consistent with regulated utilities’ obligations under
                   current Oklahoma law.

                    The Oklahoma Constitution charges the Commission with “supervising, regulating and

         controlling” transmission companies “in all matters relating to the performance of their public

         duties and their charges therefor,” and empowers it to prescribe rates, charges, classifications, and

         rules and to “require them to establish and maintain all such public service, facilities, and

         conveniences as may be reasonable and just.” 5 Title 17 of the Oklahoma statutes states that the

         Commission “shall have general supervision over all public utilities, with power to fix and

         establish rates and to prescribe and promulgate rules, requirements and regulations, affecting their




         5
             Okla. Const. art. IX, § 18.
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 110 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/30/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 17

         PUD2026-000046
         Attorney General’s Brief-in-Chief                                                     Page 4 of 17

         services, operation, and the management and conduct of their business . . .” 6 This statutory

         authority also extends to the adequacy of utility service. 7

                  The Commission’s regulatory authority described above likewise encompasses how the

         Company serves large load customers and how it acquires and integrates the resources needed to

         do so. The Commission’s rules confirm this point: no utility may furnish or charge for electric

         service “except strictly in accordance with a tariff, special contract, or rate schedule approved by

         and on file with the Commission,” 8 and no tariff or special contract is effective until approved by

         Commission order. 9

                  The Commission has jurisdiction and authority to grant the relief requested in the

         Application pursuant to Article IX, § 18 of the Oklahoma Constitution; 17 O.S. §§ 151, et seq.;

         House Bill 2992 (codified as 17 O.S. §§ 900–906); and the Commission’s rules at OAC 165:5 and

         OAC 165:35. 10

                  ACS Framework

                  The ACS framework is well within the Commission’s authority to approve, and it

         “balance[s] the needs of all parties involved.” 11 Furthermore, the ACS framework is consistent

         with the obligations of regulated public utilities under current Oklahoma law, including the duty

         to furnish adequate and reasonable service, because the resource is integrated into the Company’s

         portfolio and remains subject to Commission oversight. 12

         Attorney General’s Brief-in-Chief                                                     Page 5 of 17

                 Mr. Beling provides a high-level example of what the ACS framework could look like in

         his Responsive Testimony through a five-step approach: 1) load eligibility; 2) resource eligibility;

         3) resource evaluation; 4) process outcomes; and 5) process timeline. 13 Each step is explained in

         additional detail below.

                 Load Eligibility

                 To determine load eligibility, it must first be determined whether the load is eligible for

         service under the XLPL Tariff. Additionally, the load must meet a potential minimum megawatt

         size requirement for contract demand. The Company must also need a new resource, or new

         resources, to serve the load, i.e., the Company is not long on capacity. 14

                 Resource Eligibility

                 For a resource to be deemed eligible, the resource must be consistent with Company-

         identified needs in its latest Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”); the resource must meet Southwest

         Power Pool (“SPP”) requirements for planning capacity; the resource can be integrated into the

         Company’s system without reliability concerns; and the resource is competitive in both price and

         non-price attributes. 15

                 Resource Evaluation

                 The evaluation of the resource must be conducted by an Independent Evaluator (“IE”). The

         IE would then apply the predetermined criteria identified above in the “Resource Eligibility”

         section. Next, the IE would compare the resource pricing to a recent Company RFP process. 16

                    Process Outcomes

                    Should the IE recommend approval of the resource, the resource is deemed eligible for

         system resource handling, and the load is eligible for accelerated service to the extent made

         possible by the new resource, subject to Company approval. In contrast, if the IE recommends

         rejection of the resource, the ACS process terminates, and the load is not eligible for accelerated

         service. 17

                    Process Timeline

                    The IE would next provide a recommendation within a set number of days from the time

         of the request (for example, 60–90 days). The Company would then submit its agreement or

         disagreement with the IE recommendation within a certain number of days. If the Company and

         IE disagree, they may attempt to resolve their disagreement within a specific number of days. Any

         remaining disagreement between the Company and the IE, the Commission would resolve through

         a defined process within a set number of days. 18

         B.       The ACS framework is consistent with House Bill 2992 and the cost causation mandates
                   of Title 17, both of which govern this proceeding.

                    House Bill 2992, known as the Data Center Customer Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026

         (“Act”), is codified at 17 O.S. §§ 900–906 and took effect July 1, 2026. Although the Application

         in this Case was filed on June 17, 2026, and the Act did not take effect until July 1, 2026, the

         Attorney General maintains that the Act still applies to this proceeding. Overall, the ACS

         framework satisfies the standards codified in HB 2992 regardless of whether the Act formally

         governs a proceeding commenced before its effective date, because the better reading is that the

         Act applies to service rendered after July 1, 2026.

                 House Bill 2992 governs this proceeding; a prospective-only reading that excludes this

         proceeding would produce an absurd result.

                 Statutory interpretation “begins, as it must, with the text of the statute” and courts must

         “give effect to its plain and ordinary meaning” when that text is “clear and unambiguous.”19

         Generally, “all statutes are to be construed as having a prospective operation unless the purposes

         and intention of the Legislature to give them a retrospective effect is expressly declared, or is

         necessarily implied from the language used.” 20

                 There is a narrow exception to the rules of statutory interpretation known as the “absurdity

         doctrine” that “permits courts to depart from the unambiguous words of a statute when a plain

         reading produces patently absurd results the Legislature could not have intended,” on the

         presumption that “the Legislature did not intend the absurd result.” 21 Courts must “adopt a

         construction that promotes justice and avoids such absurdity” and does not “frustrate the

         Legislature’s intent.” 22 The Legislature “will not be presumed to have intended an absurd result,”

         and a “statutory construction which would lead to an absurdity will be avoided if this can be done

         without violating legislative intent.” 23 Although the absurdity doctrine is narrow and reserved for

         results “so gross as to shock the general moral or common sense,” exempting a data center large

         load tariff from the Data Center Customer Ratepayer Protection Act satisfies that standard. 24

                 When determining legislative intent, “the language of the entire Act should be construed

         with a reasonable and sensible construction,” and the “subject expressed in the title of the Act

         limits the scope of the Act.” 25 Legislative intent “will be ascertained from the whole [A]ct in light

         of its general purpose and objective.” 26 The legislative intent behind the Data Center Customer

         Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026 is clear in both its name and its explicit purpose stated in 17 O.S.

         § 902. The purpose of the Act is to “ensure that residential, commercial and industrial customers

         are protected from paying unjust rates resulting directly from electric service to large load

         customers.” 27 Moreover, the Commission is tasked with ensuring that “all rates are fair, just and

         reasonable, and costs and revenues are assigned and allocated among customers in accordance

         with cost causation principles.” 28

                 The Commission’s observation in the Order regarding a recent holding in a different

         proceeding that a statute that became effective after an application’s filing date did not apply

         should not compel a similar result here. 29 That observation addressed a dissimilar statute, a

         different context, and is distinguishable given both the prospective reach of House Bill 2992 to

         post-effective-date service and the Act’s express ratepayer protection purpose. Whether a statute’s

         application is prospective or retroactive “depends upon whether the conduct that allegedly triggers

         the statute’s application occurs before or after the law’s effective date.” (emphasis added). 30 The

         triggering conduct regulated under House Bill 2992 is service to large load customers and the rates

         for that service, which will occur after July 1, 2026. The June 17 filing date is an antecedent fact,

         not the trigger. Indeed, the Act’s plain text confirms this: House Bill 2992 reaches large load

         customers, defined as those adding 75 MW or more “after July 1, 2026.” 31 Applying the Act’s

         cost causation and separate tariff requirements to that future service is prospective.

                  Reading House Bill 2992 to exempt this proceeding simply because OG&E filed its

         Application shortly before July 1, 2026, would produce an absurd result the Legislature could not

         have intended. It would exempt one of the first, and largest, large load tariff proceedings in the

         State from a statute the Legislature enacted precisely to protect ratepayers from large load cost

         shifts. Nevertheless, the ACS framework is consistent with House Bill 2992 whether the Act

         applies to this proceeding or not because the framework independently honors the Act’s separate

         tariff and cost causation principles.

                  Separate tariffs for data center and computational loads (Section 903 and Section 901(4)).

                  Title 17, Section 901(4) of the Oklahoma statutes outlines a “large load customer” to

         include “new data centers, new cryptocurrency mining operations and new facilities whose

         primary function is artificial intelligence computing facilities that contract with an electric supplier

         to add 75 MW or greater” of load, “per facility or in aggregate behind a single point of

         interconnection, after July 1, 2026.” 32 Section 903 then directs that “[a]ll electric suppliers shall

         establish and maintain separate terms and conditions of electric service applicable to any large

         load customer and shall create and maintain separate tariffs applicable to such large load

         customers,” with credit requirements, recovery of costs that may remain unrecovered on departure

         or material load reduction, and a minimum ten-year term. 33 Read together, Section 903 requires

         separate tariffs for data centers and other computational large loads meeting the Section 901(4)

         threshold.

                 The Attorney General has consistently supported separate large load tariffs as both sound

         ratemaking and as consistent with the Act.34 The ACS framework operates squarely within, and

         advances the purpose of, the separate large load tariff structure contemplated by Section 903.

                 Cost Causation and Customer Affordability Charges (Section 902 and Section 901(2)).

                 Title 17, Section 902 of the Oklahoma statutes directs any governing body reviewing

         electric supplier rates to “ensure that residential, commercial and industrial customers are protected

         from paying unjust rates resulting directly from electric service to large load customers,” and that

         “all rates are fair, just and reasonable, and costs and revenues are assigned and allocated among

         customers in accordance with cost causation principles.” 35 Per the Act, “cost causation” means

         “customers responsible for the electric supplier incurring the cost should be allocated their

         equitable share of those costs.” 36

                 The ACS framework satisfies Section 902 directly: the customer brought resource and the

         costs of serving the load are integrated into the regulated portfolio and recovered through regulated

         rates, insulating other classes from stranded costs and upward rate-pressure risks. 37 By contrast,

         any charges untethered to a demonstrated cost basis oppose Section 902.

                 In his responsive testimony, Mr. Beling states that the Company is proposing a Customer

         Affordability Charge to “reduce the rates of other customers and to offset the risks of serving large

         loads.” 38 To the extent the Commission approves the Customer Affordability Charge, Mr. Beling

         recommended that it be cost-justified and that any resulting benefit be distributed among all non-

         large load customer classes rather than a single class. 39 The ACS framework is already aligned

         with cost causation principles and is designed to protect ratepayers without any need for

         reallocation or subsidization. Again, the ACS framework satisfies the standards codified in HB

         2992 regardless of whether the Act formally governs a proceeding commenced before its effective

         date.

         C.      Because the ACS framework keeps generation within the current regulated system, it
                 does not implicate the Retail Electric Supplier Certified Territory Act, Oklahoma’s
                 retail competition law, or retail wheeling.

                 The Retail Electric Supplier Certified Territory Act (“RESCTA”) divides Oklahoma into

         exclusive certified geographical territories to “encourage the orderly development of coordinated

         statewide retail electric service,” to “avoid wasteful duplication of distribution facilities,” and “for

         the public convenience and necessity and to minimize disputes . . . which may result in

         inconvenience, diminished efficiency, and higher costs in serving the consumer.” 40 Each retail

         electric supplier “shall have the exclusive right to furnish retail electric service” within its territory

         and “shall not furnish, make available, render or extend its retail electric service to a consumer for

         use” within another supplier’s territory. 41 The Oklahoma Supreme Court has expressed that

         RESCTA, “as a whole, is clearly anticompetitive” and ensures “each supplier has a monopoly in

         its respective market.” 42

                 Moreover, Oklahoma has never adopted retail electric competition or retail wheeling. The

         Electric Restructuring Act of 1997 (“Restructuring Act”) sought to explore restructuring through

         a legislative study. 43 The Restructuring Act expressly prohibited the Commission from

         “promulgating any rules or issuing any orders relating to the restructuring of Oklahoma’s electric

         utility industry without prior express authorization by the Oklahoma State Legislature,” 44 and

         suspended customer switching “until enactment of electric restructuring enabling legislation[.]”45

         A Joint Electric Utility Restructuring Task Force (“Task Force”) was created by the Restructuring

         Act to carry out the purpose of the Restructuring Act. 46 However, the Task Force had a statutory

         termination date of no later than December 1, 2009. 47 The resulting enabling legislation never

         materialized, and Oklahoma remains a vertically integrated, regulated monopoly jurisdiction.

                 The ACS framework does not disturb the requirements of RESCTA, nor does it attempt to

         operate within a retail electric competition or retail wheeling mechanism. The Company remains

         the exclusive retail electric supplier; the customer does not purchase retail electricity from a third

         party; and the customer-brought resource becomes a Company system resource rather than a

         competing retail supply. Because generation stays within the regulated system, the ACS

         framework presents none of the retail wheeling or retail competition questions raised in the Order.

         The Commission can adopt the ACS framework on narrow grounds fully consistent with RESCTA

         and existing Oklahoma law.

         D.     The Order’s remaining questions do not affect the lawfulness of the ACS framework;
                the Attorney General addresses them only as they bear on ratepayer protection.

                 Several of the Order’s questions, specifically subsections (i) through (m), arise principally

         from the AES framework proposals of other parties rather than from the ACS framework. The

         Attorney General addresses them briefly and only insofar as they bear on cost causation and

         ratepayer protection.

                 As to the Commission’s authority to set a monthly service charge where no service is yet

         provided (subsection (i)), the Commission’s plenary rate design authority is broad enough to

         authorize pre-service or reservation-type charges, provided such charges align with cost causation

         principles and are consistent with 17 O.S. § 902. 48

                 As to unbundling generation and transmission rates for transparency (subsections (j) and

         (k)), no Oklahoma statute or rule bars the Commission from directing a utility to present unbundled

         generation and transmission components within a retail tariff for transparency, and the

         Commission’s rate design authority supplies the legal basis to do so. 49 However, unbundled rate

         presentation for transparency is distinct from unbundling retail service into competitive third-party

         supply, which Oklahoma law currently does not authorize. 50 The ACS framework is fully

         compatible with transparent rate presentation. It may be further designed in such a way to fully

         satisfy the lawful desires of the Commission for additional rate design transparency, if needed.

                 As to whether it is just, reasonable, and in the public interest for a self-supplying customer

         to pay no generation demand charges while self-supplying (subsection (l)), cost causation

         principles under 17 O.S. § 902 and 17 O.S. § 901(2) require that a customer relying on the

         Company’s system be assigned and allocated its equitable share of the costs it causes. The Attorney

         General takes no position on the particulars of the other parties’ AES framework proposals but

         observes that the ACS framework avoids this concern altogether. The customer takes regulated

         service, and the brought resource becomes a system resource, so generation-related costs are

         recovered through regulated rates. 51

                    As to the considerations for bilateral, credited capacity supply (subsection (m)), the ACS

         framework itself is a structure for crediting customer-supplied capacity while protecting

         ratepayers. Should the Commission encourage such arrangements, the considerations Mr. Beling

         identifies should govern: eligibility under the XLPL Tariff tied to a demonstrated Company

         resource need; resource consistency with the Company’s IRP and with SPP planning capacity

         requirements; independent evaluation against predetermined criteria and a recent competitive

         solicitation; system integration and reliability standards; and protections, including a Company

         option to terminate, if the associated load fails to materialize, reduces, or departs the system. 52

         These conditions keep credited capacity within the regulated system and protect existing

         customers.

                    Finally, as to any other legal issues the Commission deems necessary (subsection (n)), the

         Attorney General takes the position that no further relevant legal issues need to be addressed at

         this time. However, the Attorney General reserves the right to address additional legal issues in

         future filings and/or responses.

                                                     III. Conclusion

                    The Accelerated Capacity Support framework keeps new generation within Oklahoma’s

         regulated electric system and offers a lawful, ratepayer-protective path to serve large loads. It falls

         squarely within the Commission’s constitutional and statutory authority; it does not implicate the

         Retail Electric Supplier Certified Territory Act, retail competition, or retail wheeling; and it is

         consistent with House Bill 2992 and the cost causation mandates of Title 17, both of which govern

         this proceeding. The Attorney General respectfully requests that the Commission direct OG&E to

         develop an Accelerated Capacity Support framework that includes defined eligibility
